title: Slide 1 · Language Modeling and Large Language Models
question: If a model reads the word at position three while training to predict position three, what goes wrong?
answer: The input would already contain the answer. Use earlier positions to predict position three, or shift the targets one step ahead of each input.

title: Slide 2 · Choose the units to predict
question: Could we swap the IDs of open and door without changing what the text says?
answer: Yes, if we update the encoding, decoding and any model lookup rows consistently. The assignment of numbers is a convention.

title: Slide 3 · Turn text into training pairs
question: How many next-token predictions are possible in a five-token sequence if its first token is given?
answer: Four. Positions one through four each have a next token in the sequence.

title: Slide 4 · Read the distribution over words
question: Which event would incur greater loss under this distribution, seeing desk or seeing shelf?
answer: Shelf. The model assigned it 0.1, giving a loss of about 2.303. Desk at 0.6 would cost about 0.511.

title: Slide 5 · Score a whole continuation
question: What perplexity results if a model assigns 1/4 to every observed token?
answer: The mean loss is −ln(1/4) = ln(4). Exponentiating gives 4, regardless of sequence length.

title: Slide 6 · Fit a tiny language model
question: Why should extra training on these same counts stop improving near P(desk | open) = 0.75?
answer: Raising that probability helps the three desk examples but hurts the door example. For this unconstrained row, the mean loss is minimized at the observed fractions 3/4 and 1/4.

title: Slide 7 · Choose how to decode
question: If k = 1 and the highest score is unique, can a positive temperature change the chosen token?
answer: No. Dividing all logits by the same positive number preserves their ordering. Only the highest-scoring token survives.

title: Slide 8 · Generate and score different things
question: During held-out evaluation the model prefers desk but the next recorded token is door. What goes into the next prefix?
answer: Use the recorded door for likelihood evaluation. In free generation use whichever token the decoder chose. These procedures answer different questions.

title: Slide 9 · Distinguish pretraining, adaptation and evaluation
question: A model has lower perplexity on desk notes than another model, using the same test tokens. Can we conclude it answers desk policy questions correctly?
answer: The result supports better average next-token probability on those notes. Test policy answers directly against verified records before making a claim about accuracy.

title: Slide 10 · Predict from two prefixes that end the same way
question: Suppose both input rows are changed to [2] and their original targets are kept. Could another hundred training steps let this model give desk probability 1 on one row and 0 on the other?
answer: No. In the same model with dropout off, identical inputs have identical logits. The two targets are equally frequent, so the best common prediction is [0.5, 0.5].

title: Slide 12 · From this module to the next
question: Our generator can choose between desk and door. To generate a two-pixel image instead, what must change?
answer: We must define a distribution or sampling process over pairs of pixel values. A latent variable or a sequence of denoising steps can describe dependencies between them.

title: Office hours · Why would we train with the true previous word when students ultimately see generated text?
question: Why would we train with the true previous word when students ultimately see generated text?
answer: The observed prefix defines a supervised next-token example from real text. It lets us compute likelihood. Generation deliberately feeds back the model’s own choices, so a separate generation test can reveal failures after an early mistake.

title: Office hours · Does a probability of 0.9 mean a generated sentence is 90% likely to be true?
question: Does a probability of 0.9 mean a generated sentence is 90% likely to be true?
answer: It describes a token choice conditional on this model and prefix. A familiar false statement can be an easy continuation. Compare factual claims with evidence.

title: Office hours · Can perplexities from two tokenizers be compared directly?
question: Can perplexities from two tokenizers be compared directly?
answer: Their denominators may count different units. A tokenizer that splits a word into three pieces scores three prediction steps. Fix the tokenization and scored text for the comparison, or choose a common unit such as bits per byte.

title: Exercise 1
question: With the first token given, list the inputs and targets for red door opens <end>. Use a full-prefix model.
answer: red → door; red door → opens; red door opens → <end>. The model makes three predictions.

title: Exercise 2
question: Two observed continuation tokens receive probabilities 0.8 and 0.2. Compute likelihood, mean loss and perplexity.
answer: The product is 0.16. The mean loss is −ln(0.16)/2 ≈ 0.9163. Perplexity is exp(0.9163) = 2.5.

title: Exercise 3
question: For probabilities [0.5, 0.3, 0.2], compare greedy, unrestricted sampling and top-2 sampling at temperature 1.
answer: Greedy always picks the first token. Full sampling uses the supplied probabilities. Top-2 sampling retains mass 0.8 and uses [0.625, 0.375, 0].

title: Exercise 4
question: Two candidates have probabilities 0.8 and 0.2. Apply temperature 2. Which remains the greedy choice?
answer: The odds become 2:1, so probabilities become 2/3 and 1/3. The first token remains the greedy choice.

title: Exercise 5
question: After a weight update, predicting the observed word becomes easier on training records. Design a test for whether the update helps on new requests.
answer: Hold out whole new requests before fitting, and remove duplicates from training. Score both versions on the same target tokens and compute mean loss. If the goal is correct answers, additionally judge responses against verified records.

title: Exercise 6
question: A system gets two example question-answer pairs in its prompt. A second system takes gradient steps on those pairs. Which system fine-tuned?
answer: The second system changed its weights. The first received contextual examples with fixed weights. For a fair comparison test on separate questions.
